prompt.context: Your client is a large pharmaceutical drug company. They started researching the Zika virus years ago when it was discovered in Africa and are now close to a vaccine. The vaccine needs to pass a final phase of testing to be approved by the FDA, however, the client is nearly 100% certain it will pass. Your client needs to decide if they should fund the final phase, which would last 1 year and cost $2 billion. Mass production of the vaccine could start immediately following approval.
prompt.question: Should the client fund the final phase of testing for the Zika virus vaccine?

clarifying_info.a: It is administered as a one-time shot.

clarifying_info.q: Is there patent protection for the vaccine?
clarifying_info.a: Patent protection is questionable. A US senator is writing a bill that would make patenting this vaccine impossible. A congressional decision probably won't be reached for at least a year, and the bill has high levels of public and congressional support.

The nearest competitors are about 4 years from developing a vaccine. However, if there is no patent protection, it will only take competitors 2 years from the time the vaccine is released to copy it, complete FDA testing, and bring their own version to market — so the client would have roughly 2 years of protection. It will cost competitors $1 billion to copy, test, and build facilities to produce the vaccine.

clarifying_info.q: Why is Africa not in scope?
clarifying_info.a: Zika in Africa has not been linked with microcephaly (abnormally small head), so there is very limited demand, which is why it is not in the market scope.

exhibits.title: Willingness to Pay
exhibits.shows: A chart showing the relationship between price (x-axis, $0–$30) and the percentage of population willing to pay (y-axis, 0%–100%) for two curves: Developed Countries and Developing Countries.
exhibits.data: At $20 price: ~75% of Developed Countries population willing to pay. At $10 price: ~50% of Developing Countries population willing to pay. Footnote: Pricing and willingness to pay is the same for both the adult population and parents considering the vaccine for their children.

framework: Fund final phase decision: Go / No Go
Market analysis: Size the addressable population in the Americas (developed vs. developing nations separately)
Profitability analysis: Revenue (price x volume), variable costs, fixed/initial investment, payback period
Competition analysis: Patent protection status, competitor timeline, economics of competitor entry

questions.prompt: Size the market for the Zika vaccine in the Americas.
questions.guidance: Candidate should segment the Americas into developed (~400 million people) and developing (~600 million people) countries. Apply the birth rate of 15 births per 1,000 population to estimate annual new births. Use Exhibit 1 to read off the appropriate price and willingness-to-pay for each segment. Insightful candidates will identify two sub-populations: existing population (one-time addressable market) and future annual births (recurring market). They should note that some individuals will not pay at any price (anti-vaccine stance, remote/cold locations, etc.).

math.setup: Existing population: Developed = 400M at $20/75% willing; Developing = 600M at $10/50% willing. Birth rate = 15/1,000. Annual births: Developed = 400M x 0.015 = 6M; Developing = 600M x 0.015 = 9M. Apply same willingness-to-pay percentages to births.
math.answer: 600M people addressable from existing population; ~9M additional addressable from annual births each year.

questions.prompt: Calculate the profitability of launching the vaccine. Should the client proceed with the $2B investment?
questions.guidance: Candidate should ask for variable cost per dose, production capacity, and discount rate. Key insight: the client recoups the $2B investment by end of Year 2 — making this an attractive investment. Further insight: with only 9M annual births addressable in Year 3+, the profit perpetuity ($54M/10% = $540M) is less than the $1B cost for a competitor to enter, meaning competitors have no economic incentive to enter even without patent protection. The client effectively holds a monopoly position. A candidate who reaches the monopoly conclusion without the perpetuity calculation still demonstrates strong insight.

math.setup: Production capacity = 300M doses/year. Years 1 & 2: assume 300M doses split evenly between developed and developing nations (150M each). Weighted average price = (150M x $20 + 150M x $10) / 300M = $15. Variable cost per dose = $9. Year 3+: only new births addressable = 9M doses at $15 price and $9 variable cost.
steps: Year 1 Revenue: 300M x $15 = $4,500M; Variable Cost: 300M x $9 = $2,700M; Profit: $1,800M
Year 2 Revenue: 300M x $15 = $4,500M; Variable Cost: 300M x $9 = $2,700M; Profit: $1,800M
Cumulative profit after Year 2: -$2,000M + $1,800M + $1,800M = +$1,600M (investment recouped in Year 2)
Year 3+ Revenue: 9M x $15 = $135M; Variable Cost: 9M x $9 = $81M; Annual Profit: $54M
Profit perpetuity (Year 3+): $54M / 10% = $540M — less than competitor entry cost of $1,000M

NPV check: PV Year 1 = $1,800M/1.1 = $1,636M; PV Year 2 = $1,800M/1.21 = $1,488M; PV perpetuity from Year 3 = $540M/1.21 = $446M (approx $406M in casebook); NPV ≈ -$2,000 + $1,636 + $1,488 + $406 = +$1,530M
math.answer: NPV ≈ +$1,530M. Investment recouped by end of Year 2. Competitors cannot profitably enter in Year 3+ because perpetuity value ($540M) < competitor entry cost ($1,000M), giving client a de facto monopoly regardless of patent outcome.

recommendation: The client should proceed with the $2 billion investment and the final round of FDA testing to launch the Zika virus vaccine.

The market is attractively sized (600M addressable existing population), the investment is recouped within 2 years, and the client will hold a monopoly position due to first-mover advantage — even without patent protection.
risks: Zika virus may not remain contained to the Americas, potentially attracting better-funded global competitors
Competitors may have underestimated their development timeline (currently assumed 4 years away)
Competitors could achieve lower variable costs, making market entry more attractive than current economics suggest
Congressional patent bill may pass faster than expected, though this does not materially change the investment economics
next_steps: Proceed with funding the final phase of FDA testing
Track whether Zika spreads outside the Americas, which could alter competitive dynamics
Continue monitoring the congressional patent legislation
